scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Origins trace back to English country dances documented by John Playford in 1651 and 18th-century French quadrilles.
Transmitted to North America by European settlers, African American musicians initiated the tradition of calling steps.
In the 1920s, Henry Ford promoted square dancing in US public schools, while Lloyd "Pappy" Shaw codified western traditional calls in the 1930s, paving the way for modern western square dance.

Thirty-one U.S. states have designated square dance as their official state dance.

Modern western square dance employs both traditional and modern recorded tunes.

scenes.title: The people
narration: John Playford (published *The English Dancing Master* in 1651), Henry Ford (promoted square dancing in 1920s US schools), Lloyd "Pappy" Shaw (documented callers in the 1930s), Pete Seeger (popularized folk music and square dancing in the 1940s-1950s).

Includes Traditional Square Dance (Northeast/New England, Southeast/Appalachian, Western), Modern Western Square Dance, Playford dances, Irish set dance, Scottish country dance, and continental European forms like Bekedorfer and Carré de Campagne.
Descended from Morris dance, English country dance, French quadrilles, and cotillions.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Western promenade dance is parent of English country dance: Documented by John Playford in 1651, providing foundational square set concepts.
Western promenade dance is parent of Quadrille: 18th-century French four-couple square dance that merged with English country dances.
Western promenade dance is child of Modern western square dance: Standardized variant evolved from traditional western styles between 1940 and 1960.
